# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Critical reading of Varga and Holm's comment on the Halden pilot

The first half of this comment is a valuable re-analysis. It finds real problems in the Halden pilot using the pilot's own microdata, and several of them are worse than the working paper let on. The second half does not hold up. The conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" goes beyond the authors' own numbers, rests on a weak extrapolation, and ignores the strongest evidence against it, from the very trial they cite approvingly.

I checked the arithmetic. Table 2 is correct (95.1/0.8 gives +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 gives +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 gives +10.8%), the hours falls of −14.1% and −13.9% are correct, and the real revenue figure of −2.6% is correct. Two internal inconsistencies are noted below.

## What the comment establishes

**1. The attrition finding is the most important result.** The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show that seven of the nine left after the reduced schedule had started, and six of the nine cited workload or output. This is not a matter of interpretation: the working paper misdescribed the facts. Its sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

**2. Manager ratings ran high.** In 19 of the 23 organisations with records, the manager's index exceeded the record-based index, by 3.8 points on average. That is a consistent bias in one direction, which is what you would expect when the person rating is also the sponsor.

**3. Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.** This matches Varden's figure of 13% in case-processing offices quite closely, which makes it more credible.

**4. Revenue fell in real terms.** Nominal growth of 1.4% against 4.1% inflation is a real fall of about 2.6%.

**5. The sector-general claim does not hold.** The authors make the same point I made earlier: with hours cut by 20%, any output index above 80 shows a per-hour "gain," so a gain in every sector proves nothing.

## Problems with the re-analysis

**1. The abstract claims a correction for attrition that was never made.** It says "correcting the first three" problems brings the gain down to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described but not quantified, and no bounds are given.

A rough bound is easy to compute. Suppose all nine dropouts produced output of 80, meaning no per-hour gain at all, and weight by organisation. The mean output index falls from 98.7 to about 96.3. Attrition plausibly matters, but the comment needs to estimate how much rather than imply it was folded into the 10.8%.

**2. Each row of Table 2 uses a different subset.** The four rows cover 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The fall from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore mixes the effect of the corrections with differences in which organisations are included.

The table needs one more row: the uncorrected figure for the same 17 organisations. That is, the manager-reported output for those 17, divided by 0.8. Without it, readers cannot tell how much of the drop comes from the corrections. The 23-organisation subset had a manager index of 98.9, close to the overall 98.7, so the distortion is probably small. It should still be shown.

**3. The hours breakdown does not add up.** Scheduled time was 32 hours. Adding 0.7 extra hours on each of four days and 1.6 hours on the day off gives about 36.4 hours, not the reported 34.6. The reported figure leaves only about 2.6 extra hours beyond the schedule. Either the per-day figure or the day-off figure appears to be wrong, or the two components were measured on different samples. The headline −14.1% is not affected, but this needs explaining.

**4. Organisation records are not automatically the truth.** One of the record types used is "billable hours delivered." For a professional-services firm, billable hours is itself a measure of hours. Cut working time and billable hours fall almost automatically, whatever happens to the value of the work. Ticket and case counts also ignore differences in complexity.

The fact that managers' ratings are higher in 19 of 23 cases is good evidence they skew upward. But some of the 3.8-point gap may be managers allowing for things the raw counts miss. The comment treats record-based output as the true figure without discussing this.

## Where the argument goes too far

**1. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the comment's own results.** After every correction the authors could make, a gain of 10.8% remains. The abstract says the problems account for "most" of the gain, and the data note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The conclusion then states that the gains of all "reduced-hours schemes" are entirely an artifact. That leaps from 17 organisations in one pilot to the whole field, and it erases the remaining effect.

**2. The novelty argument has three weaknesses.**

- **It extrapolates a straight line from two survey readings.** And even that line doesn't support the claim. Energy fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD over three months, which projects to zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." A curve that levels off would fit the same two points equally well.
- **It uses the wrong measure.** Self-reported energy is not output. The pilot collected the output index every month, and the authors have the microdata. If novelty were driving the gain, output per hour should fall from month three to month six. They could have tested this directly and did not.
- **A novelty effect would not be an "artifact of measurement."** It would be a real gain that may fade. The comment treats a temporary effect as if it were a fake one.

**3. It cites the Varden trial selectively.** Varden's case-processing stratum was randomised and used record-based output and timesheet hours. Those are the methods this comment recommends. It found output per actual hour up 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months, beyond the point where the authors' energy projection reaches zero.

The comment calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature" and passes over the equally reliable case-processing result from the same trial, which contradicts the conclusion. Varden's control staff knew about the trial, so a Hawthorne effect cannot be ruled out entirely. But the case-processing result is the strongest evidence available that a gain survives the corrections this comment applies.

**4. It misdescribes the meetings analysis.**

- The seven offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known." They were all of the treated case-processing offices. The meetings data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results were in.
- The Varden authors had already labelled the analysis as exploratory, warned that seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test. Telling readers not to cite it as a mechanism repeats Varden's own caveat as though it were a rebuttal.

The comment also overlooks that the meetings hypothesis competes directly with the novelty hypothesis. Removing standing meetings is a change to how work is organised, and there is no obvious reason it would fade the way novelty does. The comment needs to rule this out, not dismiss it.

**5. It has the burden of proof backwards.** Saying that a durable gain has not yet been shown is fair. Saying the gain is entirely an artifact is itself a strong positive claim, and the comment offers less evidence for it than it demands of the other side.

## Conclusions the evidence supports

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Halden's 23.4% gain is heavily overstated | Well supported |
| Halden misreported attrition | Well supported, and serious |
| The corrected gain in the subset with usable data is about 11% | Supported for that subset, with no adjustment for attrition |
| Reduced hours cut output in work that depends on staff presence | Supported (Varden counter stratum, Halden retail) |
| The remaining gain is novelty | Speculative, and testable with the monthly data the authors have |
| All per-hour gains are entirely an artifact | Not supported, and contradicted by Varden's case-processing result |

Taken together, the three papers suggest this: in work that can be queued, a real per-hour gain of perhaps 10–12% survives proper measurement for at least nine months, possibly helped by cutting low-value time. Its durability is unproven, and Varden's 24-month follow-up will be the key test. In coverage-bound work, reduced hours cost output unless more staff are hired.

The comment's methodological recommendations are sound: record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up and intention-to-treat analysis. Its conclusion should be weakened to match its own results.
